title: AI Lurches Toward Recursive Self-Improvement
dek: Elon Musk calls GrokBot's serving costs unsustainable and reignites the subsidy-era debate. Meanwhile, an MIT paper shows a frontier model editing a smaller model's weights directly, and Anthropic's updated S-1 says it may imminently hit its RSI danger threshold. The three-letter acronym is everywhere. The harder question is what it means when it arrives.

oneIdea.headline: We're so busy asking whether RSI is here that we're not asking what it means.
oneIdea.summary: Sundar Pichai expects RSI to drive acceleration over the next 12 months. MIT researchers show GPT-6 Astra rewriting a smaller model's weights. Anthropic's S-1 warns it may imminently cross its RSI danger threshold, and Wall Street is reading the charts. Yet better models aren't a straight line to revenue: enterprises still consume a vanishingly small share of available intelligence because adoption is hard. Like AGI before it, RSI risks becoming a definitional sideshow. The more useful question is what the world looks like once it arrives.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Subsidised pricing and our scribe vendors
items.body: Both sides agree usage limits are tightening and some pricing is subsidised. For a practice, that means today's scribe or AI tool price may not last. Before signing, ask about price caps, contract length, data export and what happens to patient records if the supplier is sold or fails.

items.title: Adoption, not capability, is the bottleneck
items.body: NLW says enterprises use only a sliver of available intelligence because adoption is hard. That matches primary care: the limiting factors are governance, DPIA sign-off, training and workflow, not model quality. Zitron would add that revenue built on venture money is fragile, which is a supplier-risk point rather than a clinical one.

items.title: Recursive self-improvement is not a surgery issue yet
items.body: Nothing here changes clinical practice. The sceptical reading is that the headline results came from tiny models and a bug fix. Treat claims of runaway progress with caution and judge tools on supervised, local performance.

the_other_side.text: Zitron argues the boom ends when the money runs out, because venture capital and debt fund labs whose economics do not support the spending. He says most AI subscriptions are heavily subsidised, with users consuming several dollars of compute for each dollar paid, and that providers will eventually raise prices or cut limits. He points to Musk throttling Grok Bot and OpenAI moving to token-measured limits as early signs, and says roughly 80 per cent of the two leading labs' revenue comes from venture-backed start-ups. He did not discuss recursive self-improvement.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether what users pay covers what intelligence costs to deliver. Both accept as fact that Grok Bot was throttled over cost, that usage limits are tightening, and that power users generate much of the revenue. The empirical question is how much of that spending is subsidised by investors rather than earned from customers; the observable is repricing: if users stay at honest, unsubsidised prices, Whittemore's reading holds, and if they churn, Zitron's does. The residue is worldview: whether capability gains such as recursive self-improvement will arrive fast enough to outrun the bills. For Whittemore to be vindicated, power users must keep paying API-level rates and enterprise adoption must catch up. For Zitron, repricing must trigger churn and start-up funding must tighten. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore is bullish and anti-doom, Zitron certain of a bubble and anti-hype. The signal is that each treats the subsidy era ending as real, despite opposite priors. Watch OpenAI's December token-based limits and how users respond.

headlines.headline: I would expect the next 12 months to see continued acceleration because of RSI.
headlines.attribution: Sundar Pichai, Alphabet CEO, on the company's earnings call
headlines.summary: On Alphabet's earnings call, Pichai said AI is already helping Google increase its training and launch velocity. Recursive self-improvement is no longer a fringe idea. It is showing up in CEO earnings commentary.

headlines.headline: Musk says GrokBot costs too much to serve
headlines.summary: After GrokBot users hit usage limits they had never run into before, Elon Musk replied that the cost of serving the product was unsustainably high relative to revenue. He gave no further details, but for market bears the post landed with the force of a bomb.

headlines.headline: From fastest-growing ever to unsustainable in two weeks
headlines.summary: Weeks earlier, Musk had said he'd never seen anything grow as fast as GrokBot and that the lack of a free tier proved people derived real value. Days earlier, he had posted that saving money is pointless given superintelligent abundance. Critics struggled to square either message with the new cost warning.

headlines.headline: The real anger was the unannounced change, not the limit
headlines.summary: Many users framed it as shrinkflation: they kept paying for the same plan and got less with zero notice, then were told they had picked the wrong tier. The lesson for any AI vendor tightening limits is to announce changes ahead of time so customers can adjust.

headlines.headline: Rival personal agents move to poach GrokBot users
headlines.summary: Observers called it a win for Dots and Duet. The makers of Hermes jumped in with step-by-step instructions for migrating from GrokBot to their agent.

headlines.headline: Is the problem GrokBot, or the whole personal-agent category?
headlines.summary: Dax from OpenCode argued people don't want to pay for personal agents, so they have to be top-of-funnel for something else that nobody has identified yet. This echoes the fall 2025 bubble debate over ChatGPT's costly free users, and skeptics quickly extended it to Meta, whose position in the AI race rests heavily on Muse.

headlines.headline: Bears read it as the end of the subsidy era
headlines.summary: Skeptics called it the moment the music stops: VC money runs out, prices rise, users drop off, valuations plummet. One newsletter cited an analysis estimating that a full month on a $200 ChatGPT Pro plan would cost about $14,000 at regular API prices.

headlines.headline: Loud bears make a bubble less likely, not more
headlines.summary: NLW is no AI bear, but he welcomes the skeptics. It would be far more dangerous if everyone were too enamored of Anthropic and OpenAI to ask critical questions. He also notes that bearish analysis varies widely in quality, and permabears who keep moving the goalposts may not be the best guide.

headlines.headline: Ending subsidies sorts users into two buckets, not off a cliff
headlines.summary: Some users find more efficient models good enough and stay on $20–30 plans. Others get enough value to pay for the intelligence they consume as a cost of doing business. For NLW, API spend is net new money, still far below the cost of equivalent human labor and the time to recruit and manage it.

headlines.headline: The bear case argues against itself
headlines.summary: Will users abandon AI once they pay API rates, or is revenue already too concentrated among power users who pay via the API? The two claims sit awkwardly together. The more interesting middle ground, argued by Chamath Palihapitiya, is that too many power users are still subsidized by VC dollars.

headlines.headline: Musk has a history of stoking AI market jitters
headlines.summary: He posted "Yikes" after CoreWeave's bonds had a bad day, and later claimed debt markets had almost entirely shut off for companies without substantial non-AI-data-center revenue. Some suspect 4D chess aimed at cheap acquisitions or hurting rivals, but no one knows.

headlines.headline: Meta's real personal-agent play may be small businesses
headlines.summary: a16z's Olivia Moore points to Meta's 3.64 billion daily users and more than 500 million SMBs already marketing on its platforms. Meta plans to connect Muse to ad analytics plus tools like QuickBooks and Stripe, which could make Muse a nervous system for SMBs.

headlines.headline: On economically valuable tasks, Gemini 4 wins on price
headlines.summary: SemiAnalysis's new GDPX benchmark covers tasks like chip design, finance and biology. Opus 5.5 scored highest at 12% for $51 per task, while Gemini 4 Carbon hit 10.9% for $16, roughly 4× cheaper. The labs are now focused on using efficient models to cut personal-agent costs, as they did with coding agents.

headlines.headline: OpenAI starts hill-climbing on everyday life
headlines.summary: OpenAI's LifeVal measures tasks like finding childcare, budgeting and ordering groceries. Scores rose from 49.3% for GPT-5.2 to 80.6% for GPT-6 Astra. As with coding, once a capability becomes a measured RL target it tends to improve fast and get cheaper, and some read the benchmark as a prelude to a public personal-agent launch.

headlines.headline: A frontier model edits a smaller model's weights directly
headlines.summary: MIT researchers found GPT-6 Astra could read and adjust the weights of Qwen 3.5 0.8B. By changing just 0.016% of them, it improved math benchmark scores 6× and instruction following 3×. The researchers say frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights.

headlines.headline: No gradients, no training: just 50 forward passes
headlines.summary: Asked to make Qwen better at math, Astra spotted the model's known reasoning-loop problem, located the cause within a budget of 50 forward passes, and edited it out. That boosted other capabilities too. Astra also wrote small game-playing networks from scratch that outplayed networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

headlines.headline: Replicated fast, with big caveats
headlines.summary: A senior Google researcher quickly reproduced the results and called it a step-change capability that appeared only in the latest models. The edited models are tiny, though: 20,486 parameters in his experiment, versus more than a trillion for frontier models. He frames it as 2010s-style interpretability work now done by models at a scale beyond humans.

headlines.headline: Bug fix or the mechanism of RSI?
headlines.summary: The main critique is that the 6× math gain came from fixing a loop bug, not from improving general capability. Others say the approach is undersold, reporting that Claude models can write functioning neural net weights from scratch. RSI believers argue interpretability is dual-use: models good at optimization are good at optimizing themselves.

headlines.headline: Anthropic's S-1 says the RSI danger threshold may be imminent
headlines.summary: New language in Anthropic's updated S-1 says internal estimates indicate it may soon hit its threshold of dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI: as much progress in one year as two years at the 2018–2024 pace. The company is considering responsible scaling policy updates aimed at keeping humans in control of frontier development.

headlines.headline: We do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models.
headlines.summary: The full line adds "without meaningful human supervision or understanding." It is a frontier lab, in an IPO filing, describing the limits it plans to put on AI building its own successors.

headlines.headline: Wall Street discovers "the world's most important chart"
headlines.summary: The Wall Street Journal ran Anthropic's chart showing AI now leading 26% of research, echoing Jack Clark's view that RSI might be the most important technical trend in the world. The data is from August and was boosted by David Sacks, who wondered where the number stands now. With the AI narrative souring, investors are watching RSI as a source of the next leg of growth.

headlines.headline: Better models aren't a straight line to more revenue
headlines.summary: The unspoken assumption is that improved models drive adoption. That held for true step changes like the Opus 4.5 jump that kicked off the agentic coding era. Without an entirely new capability coming online, NLW doesn't think the evidence says capability alone drives adoption.

headlines.headline: Enterprises use a sliver of available intelligence, and models aren't why
headlines.summary: Whether these business models work comes down to how much intelligence enterprises consume, and today that is a vanishingly small share of what they could. The reason is inertia, lumbering corporate systems and hard adoption, not insufficient models. The bear reading is that we aren't using it; the bull reading is that we aren't using it yet.

headlines.headline: Stop defining RSI and start imagining it
headlines.summary: The debate is stuck on whether RSI is here yet. The only group offering a vision of the world after RSI is the AI safety camp that wants it banned. Like AGI before it, the acronym may be absorbing attention that should go to understanding what it will mean when it arrives.
